overview: S32 is the server's transaction confirmation, the oldest reliable latency probe in the protocol: the server sends a transaction id, the client echoes it back, and the round trip is the ping. Modern anticheats have turned the echo into a transaction clock (Grim sends a transaction before and after sensitive packets, Hydro schedules work on frames), while classic anticheats use it as a ping spoof detector by comparing transaction latency against keep-alive latency. Because the client must echo the exact id, S32 is also where ping-spoof disablers attack the anticheat.

checks.name: PacketPingListener (Grim)
checks.purpose: Runs the transaction clock: sends transaction ids the client must echo, tracks send and receive order, and fires the transaction events the whole anticheat schedules on.
checks.how_it_works: On the OUT side, records each sent window-confirmation (negative ids Grim generates, and the ping packet on modern versions) into a sent-map and increments lastTransactionSent. On the IN side, only accepts replies whose id was actually sent, marks the transaction valid, cancels the echo to keep packet limiters happy, and fires the send/receive events that checks, setback teleports and velocity handlers all schedule against.
checks.detects: Ping-spoof disablers that echo fake transaction ids, and any client that reorders or drops transaction confirmations.
checks.variations: Hydro's TransactionTracker uses Pledge frames for the same two-phase confirmation; Frequency keeps a simple id-to-timestamp map.

checks.name: PingSpoofA (Frequency)
checks.purpose: Flags ping spoofing as a divergence between the transaction-measured ping and the keep-alive-measured ping.
checks.how_it_works: On each flying packet, reads the transaction ping (from the ConnectionManager echo map) and the keep-alive ping. If the transaction ping exceeds the keep-alive ping by more than 50ms outside lag, teleport, tps and chunk exemptions, and after the first 10 ticks, the check fails.
checks.detects: Ping-spoof modules that inflate only the transaction clock while the keep-alive clock stays honest.
checks.variations: Azure's PingSpoof sends its own random transaction ids and compares the echo delay to the reported NMS ping; both detect the same divergence.

checks.name: PingSpoof (Azure)
checks.purpose: Sends its own random transaction probes and compares the echo delay against the reported ping to expose spoofed latency.
checks.how_it_works: On the first flying packet after a transaction, sends a server-bound transaction with a random id and sets the sent flag. When the client echoes it, the check compares the round-trip delay against the player's reported NMS ping: if the reported ping is more than 2.75 times the measured delay plus 50ms, it flags with the spoofed millisecond difference.
checks.detects: Ping-spoof modules that inflate the reported ping while the real transaction echo stays fast.
checks.variations: Frequency compares two independent clocks; Azure compares the transaction clock against the server's own reported ping field.

checks.name: TransactionTracker (Hydro)
checks.purpose: Schedules anticheat work on the transaction confirmations using Pledge frames, and kicks on frame errors.
checks.how_it_works: Registers pre and post actions against Pledge frame ids: confirmPre schedules work on the first id of a frame, confirmPost on the second. When a transaction frame arrives, the tracker runs every action scheduled for that id; missing or incomplete frames are handled as error events that kick the player.
checks.detects: Transaction desync and confirmation manipulation: a client that drops or reorders confirmations produces missing or incomplete frames.
checks.variations: Grim implements the same two-phase ordering natively; Hydro outsources it to Pledge and turns frame errors into kicks.
